title: Rhyme, Alliteration and Sound
objective: After this level you can identify rhyme, slant rhyme, alliteration and assonance and how each ties words together.
summary: Rhyme matches sounds at line ends, perfectly (bright, flight) or on a slant (young, long). Alliteration repeats first consonants; assonance repeats vowel sounds.

cards.headline: Shakespeare's Sonnet 30 is full of s sounds, on purpose.
cards.body: "When to the sessions of sweet silent thought / I summon up remembrance of things past." Sessions, sweet, silent, summon. Say it aloud and the words start echoing each other. Poets have a whole kit for making words chime, and you can learn to hear every tool in it.

cards.headline: Rhyme, perfect and slant
cards.body: Rhyme is the matching of sounds, usually at the ends of lines. In a perfect rhyme, the last stressed vowel and everything after it match: bright and flight. A slant rhyme only nearly matches, like young and long. Rhyme is younger than you might think. Ancient Greek and Roman poets rarely if ever used it, and it took hold in Western poetry only in the Middle Ages. China's earliest surviving rhymes date to about the 10th century BCE.

cards.headline: Echoes at the front and in the middle
cards.body: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds, especially at the start of nearby words: sessions of sweet silent thought. Its sounds are pleasing and memorable, which is why nursery rhymes and ads love it. Assonance repeats vowel sounds in nearby words; its Latin root, assonare, means "to answer with the same sound." So rhyme ties line endings together, alliteration ties word beginnings, and assonance ties the vowels in between.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Alliteration: consonants, usually at the front. Assonance: vowels, anywhere nearby.

cards.headline: Sound: tuned
learned: Rhyme matches sounds, usually at line ends
Perfect rhyme: bright, flight. Slant: young, long

questions.prompt: Which pair of words is a slant rhyme?

options.label: Today and matter
options.rationale: Those are an iamb and a trochee.

questions.explanation: A slant rhyme only nearly matches, like young and long; bright and flight is a perfect rhyme.

questions.prompt: How does assonance tie words together?

options.label: It repeats consonants at the start of words
It repeats vowel sounds in nearby words
It matches the sounds at the ends of lines

questions.explanation: Assonance, from the Latin for "to answer with the same sound," repeats vowel sounds in nearby words.

questions.prompt: Level 31 said poems are built for the ear. Which device links "sessions," "sweet" and "silent" in Sonnet 30?

options.label: Slant rhyme
options.rationale: These words share first sounds, not endings.

questions.explanation: The repeated s at the start of sessions, sweet and silent is alliteration: repeated consonant sounds.
